narrative:
Your application for law school admission was rejected because the model predicts a 51.8% chance you'll fail the bar exam on your first try, just barely tipping over the edge into the "fail" category based on your profile. This prediction hinges heavily on your overall academic standing, particularly your Year 1 and Year 3 school deciles of 2 and 1, which lag far behind the averages of 6 and nearly 6 for students who passed the bar. While your LSAT score of 36 is close to the 37.3 average for passers, and your undergraduate GPA of 3.4 actually exceeds their 3.24 average, those strengths weren't enough to offset the lower deciles. Your lower-middle family income bracket is less common among bar passers, who are mostly upper-middle or middle class, though your full-time student status aligns well with the 93% of successful students in that category.

To understand why, imagine "what if" scenarios where we tweak just enough about your profile to flip the model's prediction to "pass," ensuring your application would get approved—these are called counterfactuals. We generated three such scenarios, and in every single one, the only change needed was a small drop in your undergraduate GPA to 3.2. None of the counterfactuals touched your school deciles, family income, LSAT, or full-time status, meaning the model sees your undergraduate GPA as the key pivot point right now.

This points to your undergraduate GPA as the most critical factor the model weighs in this borderline case—it's the feature that changed 100% of the time, by an average of just -0.2 points across all scenarios, with no other features varying at all. Your current 3.4 GPA is already a strong point compared to bar passers, so this counterintuitive sensitivity suggests the model might be interacting it uniquely with your low deciles, treating it as a confirming signal of potential risk unless adjusted slightly lower in simulation.

For actionable steps, focus on bolstering areas the model ignored but you can realistically influence, like pushing your school deciles higher through stronger performance in upcoming years, since they're stuck low now and unchanged in every scenario. Retaking the LSAT to hit 37 or above could build a buffer, given how close you are. While family income isn't movable, seeking scholarships or support networks common among upper-middle passers might indirectly help. A modest GPA tweak isn't feasible since yours is already solid, but combined academic gains elsewhere could shift the balance without it. With targeted improvements in deciles and LSAT, you'd likely flip the prediction entirely, mirroring profiles of accepted students.
